name: bone
summary: Carved bone: skull, rib and claw worked into armour plates. Hard, dry, porous, dead white where the light finds it and near black where it does not.
why: This exists because the Bone set was assigned plate_steel and went black. The set is the
Dark Wizard's second, and MU paints it dark: upper_06 means 83 and lower_06 means 57,
against the Plate set's 137. Albedo on a metal is its reflectance and there is almost no
diffuse term, so a dark sheet declared metal keeps only the highlights the artist drew and
loses every mid-tone between them - which is what 'the bone set seemed dark' was.
Metallic 0.0, and that is the first correction. Nothing in this set was forged: it is
skulls, ribs and claws over a dark hide, and the giveaway is in the sheets rather than in
the name. Chroma across all five is 2 to 5, so it is achromatic - but so is steel, and
that is why colour does not settle it. What settles it is that the shapes are grown ones.
Roughness 0.58, which is glossier than skin's 0.78 and duller than a blade. Bone that has
been worked and handled has a low sheen along its curve - the sheets draw exactly that,
a soft wide highlight down the skull's brow rather than a hard streak.
A cast grain, and this file said 'no grain' at first and was wrong. The argument then was
that the three kinds each name a process bone did not go through, and that reads the names
too literally: `cast` in this library is isotropic pitting, which is why plaster, rock and
sand all carry it and none of them was poured. Bone is porous - that is the one thing
everybody knows about it - and pitting is what porous looks like.
It also fixes something larger than taste. A material with no grain has depth 0, and
build_maps scales the whole height field by that depth before it takes the gradient - so a
grainless material throws away not only its own grain but the relief read out of MU's
painting, which is meant to be half of it. The five Bone pieces were shipping no normal map
at all: the skulls and ribs the artist carved into the sheet reached the model as colour and
nothing else, and the surface came out flat wherever it was not painted. Ten other materials
are in the same position and each wants its own look; this is the first of them.
Depth 0.10 and range 0.12, between ceramic's 0.05 and plate_steel's 0.12: deep enough that
the highlight breaks up across a pauldron, shallow enough that a skull's brow is still the
biggest thing on it. Scale 256, the finest a 1024 map can draw, because a pore is
smaller than a rivet. It asked for 340 and was capped every build; the file now says what it gets.

Grain depth 0.1 -> 0.05, and the pairing is what was wrong rather than either number. Scale 256 is the finest a 1024 map can draw and the note above is right that a pore is small - but it was combined with the deepest depth in the library, and fine plus deep is not porosity, it is noise. Measured on the shipped set the normal deviation came out at 0.11 against plate steel's 0.05 and leather's 0.02, the highest of any material here, on art whose whole subject is carved relief: the skull on the breastplate and the ribs down the skirt were being buried under pitting the sheet never had.

It was also quietly overriding the stated roughness. specular_floor raises roughness wherever the normals disagree inside a shading footprint, which is correct and is why a grain this strong never rendered at 0.58 - the set shipped at a measured 0.72, a fifth above the file's own figure, with the roughness map running to 1.00 on the helm. Halving the depth lets the number in this file be the number on the model.
